newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Patent applications rose 21.6 pct in 1996 - WIPO.
newsitem.headline: Patent applications rose 21.6 pct in 1996 - WIPO.

text.p: Some 47,291 applications for international patents were filed in 1996, a 21.6 per cent rise over the previous year, the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO) said on Friday.
American inventors and industrialists filed the lion's share of applications, some 20,828 last year, or 44 per cent, it said.

Their rivals in Germany (5,695 or 12 per cent), Japan (3,861 or 8.2 per cent), Britain (3,440 or 7.3 per cent) and France (2,307 or 4.9 per cent) followed among the top five, according to a WIPO statement.

The U.N. specialised agency administers the 1978 Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) which facilitates obtaining patent protection for inventors and industry through filing a single international application. Eight-nine states have ratified the pact, including Turkey, Israel, Cuba and Bosnia last year.
"The worldwide use of the PCT route continued to increase considerably during 1996," WIPO said in a statement.
"By filing one 'international' patent application under the PCT, protection for an invention can be sought simultaneously in each of a large number of countries," it added.
The 47,291 international applications received in 1996 had a total equivalent effect of 2.6 million national applications, it added. The figure includes the effect on regional applications.
"The WIPO share of fees will amount to some 100 million swiss francs ($71 million), representing about two-thirds of the organisation's budget," WIPO spokesman Laurent Mandelier told a news briefing.
"That shows WIPO's excellent financial health which is strongly linked to the good functioning of the PCT system for which we foresee strong growth in the coming years," he added.

WIPO cited a notable increase in the number of international applications received from major users: Japan (1,161 more than in 1995 or a 43 per cent rise); Switzerland (289 more for a 36.8 per cent rise); France (499 more or a 27.6 per cent rise); the United States (4,240 more for a 25.6 per cent rise) and the Netherlands (292 more or a 22.5 per cent rise).
On average, applicants filed for patent designations in 30.3 countries against 25.3 in 1995, it added.
Mandelier said: "The PCT allows inventors and industrialists to file a request for an international patent covering up to 89 countries instead of filing 89 national requests.
"As a result, they save a huge amount of money and time."
With effect from January 1996, certain fees were reduced by 75 per cent for international applications filed by applicants from 58 countries with a low per capita national income.
"Fees will be lowered again next year and the trend to lower fees will continue," a WIPO source told Reuters.

The Geneva-based agency sponsored negotiations last December which clinched two international treaties to extend copyright rules to protect digitally-transmitted sound recordings and the rights of performers on the Internet.
